description: Located in Nichinan, Miyazaki Prefecture, Udo Inari Shrine is a picturesque Shinto sanctuary nestled along the scenic coast. Perched near the cliffs overlooking the Pacific Ocean, it is celebrated for its striking vermilion structures, iconic torii gates, and peaceful spiritual atmosphere.

Located in Nachikatsuura, Wakayama Prefecture, Nachi Waterfall is one of Japan's tallest single-drop waterfalls, plunging 133 meters in a breathtaking natural setting. Revered as a sacred site in Shinto tradition, it forms a dramatic and iconic backdrop alongside the nearby Seiganto-ji pagoda and Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine.

Located in Hioki, Kagoshima Prefecture, this serene Inari Shrine is a traditional Shinto sanctuary dedicated to the deity of agriculture and prosperity. Nestled in a quiet area near Yunomoto Onsen, it offers visitors a peaceful atmosphere surrounded by nature and rich local history.

Located in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture, Ryuo Shrine is a tranquil Shinto sanctuary dedicated to dragon deities associated with water and protection. Surrounded by lush greenery, this historic local landmark offers a peaceful atmosphere steeped in spiritual tradition.

Located in Takaoka, Toyama Prefecture, Zuiryu-ji is a magnificent Soto Zen Buddhist temple designated as a National Treasure of Japan. Built in the 17th century by the Maeda clan, it is famed for its impressive wooden architecture, symmetrical layout, and serene gardens.

Located atop Mount Tateyama in Toyama Prefecture, Oyama Shrine Peak Sanctuary is a sacred Shinto shrine perched at an elevation of over 3,000 meters. Accessible via a mountain hike, this high-altitude sanctuary offers panoramic alpine views and a deeply spiritual atmosphere in one of Japan's most revered holy mountains.

Located in Takachiho, Miyazaki Prefecture, Amanoiwato Shrine is a revered Shinto sanctuary dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu and tied to Japanese mythology. Built near the sacred cave where she is said to have hidden, it features scenic trails leading to the stone-stacked Amano Yasukawara cavern.

Located on Miyajima Island in Hiroshima Prefecture, Itsukushima Shrine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site famous for its iconic "floating" Torii gate and boardwalk piers built over the water. Dedicated to the three daughters of Susanoo-no-Mikoto, this 6th-century Shinto sanctuary is celebrated as one of Japan's most picturesque coastal landmarks.

Located in Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture, Atsuta Jingu is one of Japan's most important Shinto shrines, dating back over 1,900 years. Nestled in a peaceful wooded park, it is renowned for housing Kusanagi no Tsurugi, the sacred sword that forms part of the Imperial Regalia of Japan.

Located in Okayama, Okayama Prefecture, Kibitsu Shrine is a historic Shinto complex famous for its impressive 360-meter-long covered wooden corridor and unique kibitsu-zukuri roof architecture. Closely linked to the folk legend of Momotaro, the shrine's main hall is designated as a National Treasure of Japan.

Located at the foot of Mount Iwaki in Hirosaki, Aomori Prefecture, Iwakiyama Shrine is an ancient Shinto sanctuary often called the "Nikko of the Tsugaru region" for its ornate, lacquer-painted wooden architecture. Surrounded by lush cedar forests, its grand approach features impressive traditional gates framing sweeping views of the sacred mountain peak.

Located in Tsugaru, Aomori Prefecture, Takayama Inari Shrine is famous for its striking garden featuring hundreds of vibrant red torii gates winding through landscaped ponds. Dedicated to the deities of agriculture and maritime safety, it offers scenic views and a tranquil atmosphere surrounded by fox statues (kitsune).

Located on the volcanic slopes of Mount Osore in Mutsu, Aomori Prefecture, Osorezan Bodaiji Temple is a famous Buddhist temple situated beside Lake Usori, revered as one of Japan's most sacred sites for honoring departed souls. Surrounded by sulfuric steams, rock mounds, and thermal hot springs, it offers a dramatic and otherworldly atmosphere deeply rooted in local spiritual lore.

Located in Higashiyama Ward, Kyoto, Sanjūsangen-dō is a renowned 12th-century Buddhist temple famous for its 120-meter-long main hall—Japan's longest wooden structure. It houses an astounding collection of 1,001 life-sized statues of Kannon, the goddess of mercy, sculpted from Japanese cypress and gilded in gold leaf.

Located atop a coastal island in Hachinohe, Aomori Prefecture, Kabushima Shrine is dedicated to Benzaiten and famous as a breeding sanctuary for thousands of black-tailed gulls (umineko). Perched overlooking the Pacific Ocean, it offers dramatic coastal views and a unique spiritual setting where the birds are revered as sacred messengers.

Located in Kashima, Ibaraki Prefecture, Kashima-jingū is an ancient and prominent Shinto sanctuary dedicated to Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, the deity of martial arts and swordsmanship. Set within expansive, serene woods, the complex features a striking red-lacquered Romon gate, sacred deer roaming the grounds, and the legendary Kaname-ishi keystone believed to subdue earthquakes.

Located on Awaji Island in Hyogo Prefecture, Izanagi Shrine is considered one of Japan's oldest Shinto sanctuaries, dedicated to the creator deities Izanagi and Izanami. Set within peaceful wooded grounds, it features sacred ancient camphor trees and holds a central place in Japanese mythology as the dwelling where Izanagi spent his final days.

Located in Sasaguri, Fukuoka Prefecture, Nanzoin Temple is a prominent Shingon Buddhist site renowned for housing one of the world's largest bronze statues of a reclining Buddha. Nestled in a lush hillside setting, the temple complex features scenic forested paths, numerous stone statues, and serves as the starting location for the famous Sasaguri pilgrimage route.

Located in Kami Town, Hyogo Prefecture, Choraku-ji is a temple famously home to the Tajima Daibutsu, featuring three monumental golden Buddha statues set within a vast main hall. Surrounded by tranquil mountain scenery, the complex includes a tall wooden five-story pagoda and thousands of smaller gilded Buddhist figures along its walls.

Located in Kita Ward, Kyoto, Kinkaku-ji, officially known as Rokuon-ji, is an iconic Zen Buddhist temple famous for its top two floors entirely covered in gold leaf. Overlooking a scenic mirror pond and surrounded by classic Japanese gardens, it stands as one of Japan's most celebrated historic landmarks and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Located in Nikko, Tochigi Prefecture, Nikko Toshogu Shrine is a lavishly decorated Shinto complex and UNESCO World Heritage Site dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa shogunate. Nestled in a majestic cedar forest, it features intricate wood carvings, gold leaf embellishments, and iconic architectural structures such as the Yomeimon Gate and the Three Wise Monkeys.

Located along the dense forest shores of Lake Ashi in Kanagawa Prefecture, Hakone Shrine is an ancient Shinto sanctuary famous for its iconic red torii gate rising dramatically out of the water. Tucked away beneath towering cedar trees, it offers a tranquil spiritual atmosphere and historic connections to samurai leaders seeking blessings for victory and good fortune.

Located in Fujinomiya, Shizuoka Prefecture, Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha is the head shrine for over 1,300 Sengen shrines across Japan, historically dedicated to worshiping Mount Fuji and protecting against volcanic eruptions. Part of the Mount Fuji UNESCO World Heritage Site, it features distinctive two-story shrine architecture, cherry blossom-lined grounds, and a crystal-clear sacred pond fed by snowmelt from the mountain.

Located in Tarui, Gifu Prefecture, Nangu Taisha is a distinguished Grand Shinto Shrine historically regarded as the chief sanctuary of ancient Mino Province and dedicated to the deity of mining and metalworking. Rebuilt during the early Edo period under the patronage of the Tokugawa shogunate, the shrine complex is renowned for its vibrant vermilion structures, classic Momoyama-style architectural details, and rich collection of sacred swords.

Located in Nachikatsuura, Wakayama Prefecture, Kumano Nachi Taisha is one of the three sacred Kumano Sanzan grand shrines and a core site within the UNESCO World Heritage Kumano Kodo pilgrimage network. Situated high on Mount Nachi, it offers striking views of Nachi Falls—Japan's tallest uninterrupted waterfall—and features vibrant vermilion halls that embody centuries of syncretic Shinto and Buddhist worship.

Located on Nishinoshima in the Oki Islands of Shimane Prefecture, Takuhi Shrine is an ancient mountain sanctuary whose main hall is built partially inside a natural sea cave on Mount Takuhi. Historically worshipped as a patron deity for maritime safety and navigation by sailors on the Sea of Japan, the shrine features classic Edo-period architecture and holds the title of the oldest surviving shrine building in the Oki archipelago.

Located in Dazaifu, Fukuoka Prefecture, Dazaifu Tenman-gū is one of Japan's principal Shinto shrines dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, the deity of scholarship and learning. Set amidst sprawling grounds featuring thousands of sacred plum trees (tobiume) and historic vermilion bridges, the shrine serves as a major cultural landmark and a premier site for students seeking academic success.

Located in Izumo, Shimane Prefecture, Izumo Taisha is one of Japan's oldest and most important Shinto shrines, dedicated to Okuninushi no Mikoto, the deity of matchmaking and marriage. Renowned for its monumental Taisha-zukuri architectural style and colossal shimenawa (sacred straw rope), the shrine is central to Japanese myth as the gathering place for millions of Shinto deities every autumn.

Located in Kashima, Saga Prefecture, Yūtoku Inari Shrine is counted among Japan's three major Inari shrines, dedicated to the deities of agriculture, commercial prosperity, and family fortune. Founded in 1687, the shrine is celebrated for its striking vermilion main hall elevated on tall wooden stilts along a steep hillside, vibrant landscaped gardens, and a scenic trail of red torii gates leading up the mountain.

Located in Kanoya, Kagoshima Prefecture, Jintoku Inari Shrine is a distinctive Shinto sanctuary originally founded in 1676 and completely rebuilt in 2018. Combining centuries-old Inari worship with striking modern design, the shrine grounds feature a rare transparent glass torii gate alongside a traditional tunnel of vibrant vermilion senbon torii.

Located in Niimi, Okayama Prefecture, Saidouji Temple is a mountain sanctuary originally founded in 811 by Kobo Daishi and historically associated with prayers for safe childbirth and local Hoso pottery origins. Nestled amidst lush hills, the site is widely celebrated for its striking tunnel of 78 pure white torii gates (Hakuryumon) and thousands of hydrangeas and irises that bloom across the grounds each summer.

Located in Dazaifu, Fukuoka Prefecture, Tenkai Inari Shrine is a serene auxiliary sanctuary tucked into the hills behind Dazaifu Tenmangu. Revered for bringing good fortune, business success, and protection from misfortune, the shrine is reached via a stone staircase framed by vibrant red torii gates and lined with traditional flags.

Located in Nagato, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Motonosumi Shrine is a striking seaside sanctuary famous for its winding pathway of 123 vibrant red torii gates that frame dramatic views of the Sea of Japan. Established in 1955 following a divine revelation from a white fox spirit, the shrine is revered for granting success in business, maritime safety, and matchmaking, and is unique for its offering box mounted high atop the outermost entrance torii gate.

Located in Nishi Park in Fukuoka, Fukuoka Prefecture, Nakatsukasa Magotaro Inari Shrine is an intriguing Shinto sanctuary dating back to the Kamakura period, revered for bringing business prosperity and protection. Tucked into the lush hillside near Terumo Shrine, the historic site features stone fox guardians and a traditional red torii approach that has gained modern fame for its vibrant evening illuminations.

Located in Goshogawara, Aomori Prefecture, Sannobohiyoshi Shrine is a tranquil sanctuary situated within the nationally designated Sannobō Historic Site. Surrounded by dense forest and centuries-old stone lanterns, the shrine grounds preserve medieval temple foundation ruins that reflect a rich historical tradition of Shinbutsu-shūgō (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) on the Tsugaru Peninsula.

Located in Takasago, Hyogo Prefecture, Oushiko Shrine is an ancient sanctuary renowned as the home of the Ishi-no-Hoden, a colossal Megalith carved from tuff that appears to float above a stone reservoir. Revered as one of Japan's three mysterious wonders, the shrine is dedicated to the deities Ōkuninushi and Sukunabikona and has drawn worshippers seeking health, safety, and divine protection since antiquity.

Located in Hisayama, Fukuoka Prefecture, Ino Tensho Kodaijingu Shrine is a historic Shinto sanctuary fondly known as the "Ise Grand Shrine of Kyushu" due to its deep spiritual links and shared architectural traditions with Ise Jingu. Surrounded by serene forests and pristine streams, the shrine is dedicated to Amaterasu Omikami and is famed for practicing the traditional Shikinen Sengu, the periodic rebuilding of its sacred structures.

Located on Omishima Island in Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Oyamazumi Shrine is an ancient Shinto sanctuary long revered as the supreme guardian shrine for mariners, warriors, and the Seto Inland Sea. Encircled by a sacred grove of ancient camphor trees—including one estimated to be over 2,600 years old—the shrine houses a renowned treasure hall containing the vast majority of Japan's designated National Treasure and Important Cultural Property samurai armor and weaponry.

Located in Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture, Tamura Shrine is the historic Ichinomiya (principal Shinto shrine) of former Sanuki Province, dedicated to deities of water, agriculture, and local prosperity. Encircled by sacred streams and vibrant grounds, the shrine features a rich array of elaborate stone carvings, unique statues, and a revered inner sanctuary built over a sacred well.

Located atop a hill near Dogo Onsen in Matsuyama, Ehime Prefecture, Isaniwa Shrine is a magnificent Shinto sanctuary constructed in the rare Hachiman-zukuri architectural style, designated as an Important Cultural Property of Japan. Rebuilt in 1667 by the local Matsudaira clan, the shrine features a striking vermilion-lacquered complex adorned with intricate gold leaf details, historic samurai armor offerings, and panoramic views over the city.

Located in Kochi, Kochi Prefecture, Tosa Shrine is the historic Ichinomiya (principal Shinto shrine) of former Tosa Province, celebrated for its ancient origins and deep connection to the regional samurai heritage. Rebuilt in 1570 by the warlord Chosokabe Motochika, the sanctuary features a unique "蜻蛉造" (tonbo-zukuri or dragonfly-style) architecture designated as an Important Cultural Property, nestled within a tranquil forest of ancient trees.

Located in Uki, Kumamoto Prefecture, Einoo Tsurugi Shrine is a Shinto sanctuary founded in 713 and dedicated to Wadatsumi no Kami, the god of the sea. It is famed for its torii gate standing directly in the Yashiro Sea, reachable on foot at low tide and strikingly lit at sunset. The shrine is also known for its unique stingray-shaped ema votive tablets and its link to the Shiranui, a rare mirage phenomenon that appears off the coast in late summer.

Located in Itoshima, Fukuoka Prefecture, Sakurai Futamigaura is a sacred coastline within Genkai Quasi-National Park, tied to nearby Sakurai Shrine where the deities Izanagi and Izanami are enshrined. Its twin Meoto Iwa, or wedded rocks, joined by a massive shimenawa rope replaced each spring, rise from the sea about 150 meters offshore, framed by a pure white torii gate whose base submerges at high tide. Ranked among Japan's 100 best sunset views, it is especially renowned as a symbol of marital harmony.

Located in Takashima, Shiga Prefecture, on the western shore of Lake Biwa, Shirahige Shrine is considered the oldest shrine in the Omi region, founded roughly 2,000 years ago. Dedicated to Sarutahiko Okami, a deity of longevity and guidance, it is nicknamed the Itsukushima of Omi for its vermilion torii gate that appears to float on the lake, with Okinoshima island visible behind it. The gate is especially striking at sunset and is illuminated on weekend evenings.

Located on Tsushima Island, Nagasaki Prefecture, near Mount Izu, Kaijin Shrine, also known as Watatsumi Shrine, is dedicated to the sea deities Toyotama-hime and Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, whose marriage is said to have taken place here. Ranked as the highest shrine of the former Tsushima province and classified as a Beppyo shrine for its historical significance, it is believed to be among the oldest shrines in Japan. Its torii gates extending toward the sea are often compared to those of the famous Itsukushima Shrine.

Located in Yanai, Yamaguchi Prefecture, Inariyama Shrine is known for its vermilion torii gate tunnel climbing the wooded hillside, echoing the more famous Motonosumi Inari Shrine further along the coast. Dedicated to Inari Okami, the deity of rice, prosperity, and business success, its hilltop approach offers sweeping views over the surrounding Yamaguchi countryside.

Located across Kagoshima Bay in Kagoshima Prefecture, Sakurajima is one of Japan's most active stratovolcanoes and a site of deep cultural, geological, and spiritual significance. Surrounded by lush natural scenery and lava fields, the mountain features multiple observation points and sacred local shrines, such as the Kurokami Buried Torii, which stands as a dramatic reminder of the landmark's massive 1914 eruption.

Located in Hirosaki, Aomori Prefecture, Mount Iwaki is a sacred stratovolcano affectionately known as Tsugaru Fuji due to its symmetrical conical shape. A central site of mountain worship (sangaku shinko) for centuries, it hosts the historic Iwaki Shrine at its base and serves as the destination for the annual Oyama-kamairi pilgrimage.

Situated in the Philippine Sea, Aogashima is a remote volcanic island administered by Tokyo and famous for its rare double-caldera geological formation. A sacred and isolated island rich in local folklore, it features an active inner crater (Maruyama) surrounded by rugged coastal cliffs and geothermal vents used for cooking and traditional salt production.

Located in Tottori Prefecture, Daisen is the highest peak in the Chugoku region and a sacred stratovolcano long revered as a home of Shinto deities. Centered around Daisen-ji Temple and Ogamiyama Shrine, the mountain serves as a major historic hub for mountain asceticism (Shugendo) amidst sprawling beech forests and dramatic alpine slopes.

Located in Amakusa, Kumamoto Prefecture, Ushibuka Haiya Bridge is a modern architectural masterpiece designed by Renzo Piano, sweeping gracefully over Ushibuka Port. Built with an elegant, aerodynamic curve to minimize wind resistance, the structure beautifully blends contemporary civil engineering with the scenic coastal landscape while honoring the region's historic maritime heritage.

Located in Tsuruta, Aomori Prefecture, Tsuru no Maihashi Bridge is Japan's longest triple-arch wooden bridge, spanning 300 meters across Tsugaru Fujimi Lake. Completed in 1994, it was built from over 700 Aomori cypress logs more than 150 years old, using traditional Japanese carpentry techniques. Its three sweeping arches evoke a pair of cranes taking flight, framed by views of Mount Iwaki, known locally as Tsugaru Fuji, and local legend holds that crossing the bridge brings long life.

Located in Naha, Okinawa Prefecture, Shuri Castle was the royal palace and political center of the Ryukyu Kingdom from 1429 to 1879, blending Japanese, Chinese, and Southeast Asian architectural influences. Though its main hall has burned down and been rebuilt several times, most recently after a 2019 fire, the site remains part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Gusuku Sites of the Ryukyu Kingdom. Its vermilion Seiden hall and Shureimon Gate stand as enduring symbols of Okinawan cultural identity.

Located in Himeji City, Hyogo Prefecture, Himeji Castle is Japan's most celebrated feudal fortress and one of the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Sites, listed in 1993. Nicknamed Shirasagi-jo, or White Heron Castle, for its brilliant white plastered walls resembling a bird in flight, its main keep dates to 1609 and remains remarkably original, having survived earthquakes, fires, and WWII bombing raids largely unscathed. With 83 buildings and an elaborate defensive maze of gates and passages, it is widely regarded as the finest surviving example of Japanese castle architecture.

Located in Hirosaki, Aomori Prefecture, Hirosaki Castle was built in 1611 by the Tsugaru clan, who ruled the domain for 260 years until feudal rule ended in 1871. Its original five-story keep burned down after a lightning strike in 1627 and was rebuilt as the current three-story tower in 1810, making it Tohoku's only surviving Edo-period castle keep. Set within Hirosaki Park amid a triple moat, the castle is especially renowned for its cherry blossoms each spring and illuminated snow lantern festival in winter.

Located in Naka Ward, Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture, Nagoya Castle was built in 1610 on the order of Tokugawa Ieyasu to secure the Owari region, becoming the seat of the Owari Tokugawa clan, one of the three senior Tokugawa branch families. It is famed for the golden shachihoko, mythical tiger-headed dolphin ornaments believed to ward off fire, that crown its main keep and have earned the castle the nickname Kinshachi-jo. The original keep was destroyed in a 1945 air raid and rebuilt in concrete in 1959, while the Honmaru Palace was meticulously reconstructed in wood with gold-leaf interiors, reopening in 2018.

Located in front of the Kumamoto Prefectural Government Office in Chuo Ward, Kumamoto City, this bronze statue depicts Monkey D. Luffy, captain of the Straw Hat Pirates from Eiichiro Oda's One Piece. Unveiled in 2018, it was the first of ten statues placed across Kumamoto Prefecture as part of the ONE PIECE Kumamoto Revival Project, funded by Oda, a Kumamoto native, to support recovery after the 2016 earthquakes. The statue has become a pilgrimage site for manga and anime fans from around the world.

Located in Kunisaki, Oita Prefecture, this pair of weathered stone Nio guardian statues stands along a forest path among towering cedars, part of the Thirty Buddhas (Sanjubutsu) associated with the Kunisaki Peninsula. The peninsula is renowned for hundreds of rock-carved and stone Buddhist images scattered through its forests and cliffs, remnants of the ancient Rokugo Manzan tradition that fused Shinto mountain worship with Buddhism.

Located in Takachiho Town, Miyazaki Prefecture, Takachiho Gorge is a narrow basalt canyon carved by the Gokase River through lava from an ancient Mount Aso eruption, with columnar cliff walls reaching 80 to 100 meters. Its centerpiece, Manai Falls, drops 17 meters directly into the gorge and is ranked among Japan's top 100 waterfalls. Visitors can rent rowboats to glide along the emerald water beneath the cliffs, making it one of Kyushu's most iconic scenic spots.

Located in Shari, Hokkaido, along National Route 334 on the way to the Shiretoko Peninsula, Oshinkoshin Falls is ranked among Japan's 100 best waterfalls. Nicknamed the Twin Beauties Waterfall because its stream splits into two distinct cascades partway down a rugged 80-meter cliff, its Ainu name means where Sakhalin spruce grow in clusters. A stairway climbs partway up the falls for a close view of the rushing water, with the Sea of Okhotsk visible from the top.

Located in Nanto, Toyama Prefecture, Gokayama is a UNESCO World Heritage village celebrated for its gassho-zukuri farmhouses, whose steep thatched roofs were built to withstand heavy snowfall. Long isolated by surrounding mountains, the Suganuma and Ainokura hamlets preserve houses up to 400 years old, historically sustained by silk cultivation, washi papermaking, and gunpowder production. Together with nearby Shirakawa-go, Gokayama forms one of Japan's most iconic traditional mountain landscapes.

Located in Nagakute, Aichi Prefecture, Ghibli Park is the world's only official Studio Ghibli theme park, opened in November 2022 within the grounds of the former Expo 2005. Rather than thrill rides, it offers life-size recreations of scenes from beloved Ghibli films, including Satsuki and Mei's House from My Neighbor Totoro, the witch's house from Kiki's Delivery Service, and a towering reproduction of Howl's Moving Castle. Spread across five themed areas set within forest and parkland, it draws around 1.8 million visitors a year.

Located in Biei, Hokkaido, Shirogane Blue Pond formed by accident during construction of a dam built in 1988 to protect the town from volcanic mudflows off Mount Tokachi. Its striking cobalt-blue color comes from colloidal aluminum hydroxide carried by mineral-rich groundwater from nearby Shirahige Falls mixing with the Biei River, scattering sunlight in a way that shifts from milky turquoise to deep blue with the light and season. Pale trunks of dead larch trees rise from the still water, and the pond gained worldwide fame after being featured as an official Apple OS X wallpaper in 2012.

Located in Semboku, Akita Prefecture, Lake Tazawa is Japan's deepest lake at 423.4 meters, a nearly circular caldera lake with a shoreline of about 20 kilometers. Its extreme depth keeps it from ever freezing, and its clear water shifts between lapis blue and indigo with the seasons. The lake is tied to the legend of Princess Tatsuko, who drank from a cursed spring seeking eternal beauty and was transformed into a dragon, now commemorated by a golden statue on its western shore, while the vermilion torii of Goza-no-ishi Shrine marks the lake's northern point.

Located at Cape Oto on the northwestern tip of the Itoshima Peninsula, Fukuoka Prefecture, Keya no Oto is one of Japan's three largest basalt caves, carved by the Genkai Sea into towering hexagonal and octagonal columnar rock formations. Designated a National Natural Monument, the cave rises 64 meters high, stretches 90 meters deep, and is only accessible by sightseeing boat from Keya Fishing Port between March and November. A short coastal hike also leads to a clifftop viewpoint overlooking the cave and the surrounding Genkai Quasi-National Park.
